lines.text: I'm my own crew, me. Nobody's bought a stick off me since the back end of last year.
My back went two summers ago. I can still put a tree down exactly where I want it. I just can't get myself up off the ground after. My wife stopped asking how the day went, so I tell her anyway.
The Barkhide don't come up the north side. Below the town they eat the low growth back to the dirt, and on ground like that I can walk a log down to the road with one hand on it.
I've not had a saw out past the east stair in four years. The canopy up there is thinner than it was when we were cutting under it.
No Barkhide on those slopes now. The low growth has come right up over the ground, and the young trees under it all came on in the one season. There's not a stick in there worth me walking in for.
Grown Webvern silk, I can tell through a glove. Both hands on a strand and pull as hard as I like, it doesn't go. Young stuff comes apart on the frame while you wind it.
Big frame wobbled all winter. I said so the once and it was mended inside the week.

The stallholder's lad goes round the market telling people the moths make the silk. The moths make no silk. It's Webvern that make it, up in the high lines. My frame's stood idle since I came out here.
When the moths come through the lamps go out, poof, poof, poof. One went down my collar and I had it in both hands and then the stall man shouted and it got away.
Gloomgrub are the little ones and they go up in the high lines and come back down big as my hand with the wings on, and that's where the silk comes off them. I'm not allowed up the east stair.
I mind the stall man's stall while he gets his supper. Got a copper?
I was born on the floor, I raised my family on the walk, and I am in the canopy now.

In my day a man could stand on the floor and see clear across. It has grown over a great deal since. The Mosslet were down there then and they are down there still, and the Sporantle come up in what falls off the walk.
The lampkeeper was a boy on the floor when I was a married man up on the walk. I could take you through the whole of his family if you have an afternoon.
First the lower run. Forty-one, forty-two, forty — no. Lost my place. Back down to the first lamp and start again. Most nights now. Most nights.
Oil's in the shed behind the winding house. — Was it oil you wanted?

Pell has the road past the stair, and people say his is the harder one. I've not asked him. In autumn the moths put the lamps out behind me, so I light the two hundred and eleven and light most of them again.
We cut marked stands and nothing else. The marks come down from the town. It's in the crew book if you want the wording.
Two hours out at the start of the day, two hours back at the end. That's in the terms.
Webvern in the tops over this stand, so we cut round those trees. The reason given is that the silk pays better than the timber. Off the stand by dusk, and the reason given for that is the Duskstalk.
